scenes.visual: Open on the exact same cell cross-section and colour map from the first film, widened slightly to show two distinct cytokine receptors side by side in the plasma membrane above the cytoplasm and violet (#A78BFA) DNA helix. Gentle ambient drift keeps the scene alive. Overlay crisp white title: 'Receptor Tails, Specificity, and Brakes'.

scenes.tts: The first film traced one direct relay from cytokine receptor to DNA. How do four Jaks and seven Stats serve dozens of cytokines, keep their signals apart, and shut off? The answers sit in two places: the receptor tails and the cell's brakes.
scenes.caption: The first film traced one direct relay from cytokine receptor to DNA. How do four JAKs and seven STATs serve dozens of cytokines, keep their signals apart, and shut off? The answers sit in two places: the receptor tails and the cell's brakes.
scenes.visual: Title fades. Show a brief glowing trace of the direct relay from the first film, then reveal four labelled JAK blocks (JAK1, JAK2, JAK3, TYK2 in coral-red shades around #EF4444) and seven compact emerald-teal (#10B981) STAT blocks neatly arrayed beside a fan of many amber (#F59E0B) cytokine ovals arriving from above. Highlight two glowing brackets on the cell: 'Receptor tails' and 'Brakes'.
scenes.narration: The first film traced one direct relay from cytokine receptor to DNA. How do four JAKs and seven STATs serve dozens of cytokines, keep their signals apart, and shut off? The answers sit in two places: the receptor tails and the cell's brakes.

scenes.tts: Start at the membrane, where receptor tails do most of the sorting. Each receptor chain holds a particular Jak near the membrane. Farther down, its tail carries distinct docking tyrosines. The amino acids around each phosphotyrosine select which Stat's S H two domain fits.
scenes.caption: Start at the membrane, where receptor tails do most of the sorting. Each receptor chain holds a particular JAK near the membrane. Farther down, its tail carries distinct docking tyrosines. The amino acids around each phosphotyrosine select which STAT's SH2 domain fits.
scenes.visual: Zoom onto two distinct receptor pairs embedded side by side in the plasma membrane: left pair in slate blue (#3B82F6), right pair in indigo-cyan (#06B6D4). Each tail shows a distinct shaped bracket near the membrane holding its own JAK, and gold (#FACC15) 'P' tags flanked by differently shaped geometric notches below. Two differently notched STAT blocks (emerald teal #10B981 and mint teal #34D399) drift up; each fits only its matching tail notch. Label: 'Tail selects JAK and STAT'.
scenes.narration: Start at the membrane, where receptor tails do most of the sorting. Each receptor chain holds a particular JAK near the membrane. Farther down, its tail carries distinct docking tyrosines. The amino acids around each phosphotyrosine select which STAT's SH2 domain fits.

scenes.tts: Compare two receptors side by side. The erythropoietin receptor holds Jak two on its tails to drive red blood cell production. A different receptor chain in immune cells holds Jak three instead. Different tails assign different Jaks to different jobs.
scenes.caption: Compare two receptors side by side. The erythropoietin receptor holds JAK2 on its tails to drive red blood cell production. A different receptor chain in immune cells holds JAK3 instead. Different tails assign different JAKs to different jobs.
scenes.visual: Label the left slate-blue receptor 'EPO receptor' with coral-red (#EF4444) blocks labelled 'JAK2' and a small downstream icon labelled 'Red blood cells'. Label the right indigo-cyan receptor 'Immune receptor' with crimson-coral (#F97316) blocks labelled 'JAK3' and a downstream icon labelled 'Immune cells'. Amber cytokines bind each receptor, activating each dedicated JAK and sending its matched STAT pair downward.
scenes.narration: Compare two receptors side by side. The erythropoietin receptor holds JAK2 on its tails to drive red blood cell production. A different receptor chain in immune cells holds JAK3 instead. Different tails assign different JAKs to different jobs.

scenes.tts: The four Jaks look very similar in sequence. You might expect them to cover for one another when one is missing. Suppose a mouse embryo lacks Jak two completely. Will the other three Jaks step in for erythropoietin, or will that pathway fail?
scenes.caption: The four JAKs look very similar in sequence. You might expect them to cover for one another when one is missing. Suppose a mouse embryo lacks JAK2 completely. Will the other three JAKs step in for erythropoietin, or will that pathway fail?
scenes.visual: Fade out the JAK2 blocks on the left EPO receptor, leaving dashed empty outlines on its tails labelled 'No JAK2'. Keep JAK1, JAK3, and TYK2 clearly visible and intact elsewhere along the membrane and cytoplasm. An amber (#F59E0B) EPO oval binds the left receptor chains, bringing them together while the empty JAK2 sockets sit bare.
scenes.narration: The four JAKs look very similar in sequence. You might expect them to cover for one another when one is missing. Suppose a mouse embryo lacks JAK2 completely. Will the other three JAKs step in for erythropoietin, or will that pathway fail?

scenes.visual: Hold the bound EPO receptor with empty dashed 'No JAK2' sockets while intact JAK1, JAK3, and TYK2 drift gently nearby without docking. Display a high-contrast question card at top: 'Will other JAKs substitute for JAK2?' Maintain subtle ambient particle motion through the 4.5-second pause.

scenes.tts: That pathway fails. Without Jak two, mouse embryos make an early wave of red cells, but none of the lasting, adult kind. The other three Jaks remain intact, yet on this receptor tail they do not substitute.
scenes.caption: That pathway fails. Without JAK2, mouse embryos make an early wave of red cells, but none of the lasting, adult kind. The other three JAKs remain intact, yet on this receptor tail they do not substitute.
scenes.visual: Question card fades. The nearby JAK1, JAK3, and TYK2 bounce softly away from the EPO tail without binding; the receptor tails stay unphosphorylated and the red-cell signal line dims with a clean label: 'No adult-type red cells'. Briefly show a small side note badge: 'STAT5A & 5B partly overlap', keeping the hedge visible alongside 'JAK2 is not replaced'. Empathy fix: Label the empty red-cell slot 'No lasting (adult-type) red cells'. The STAT5 overlap is now on screen only, as a small badge 'STAT5A & 5B partly overlap'.
scenes.narration: That pathway fails. Without JAK2, mouse embryos make an early wave of red cells, but none of the lasting, adult kind. The other three JAKs remain intact, yet on this receptor tail they do not substitute.

scenes.tts: Now ask how a healthy signal turns off. Two main brakes do most of that work. First, tyrosine phosphatases strip phosphates from Jaks, receptor tails, and Stats. Once a Stat loses its phosphate in the nucleus, it returns to the cytoplasm, ready for reuse.
scenes.caption: Now ask how a healthy signal turns off. Two main brakes do most of that work. First, tyrosine phosphatases strip phosphates from JAKs, receptor tails, and STATs. Once a STAT loses its phosphate in the nucleus, it returns to the cytoplasm, ready for reuse.
scenes.visual: Restore the active glowing pathway with phosphorylated JAK2, receptor tails, and emerald-teal STAT pairs on violet DNA. Cool cyan-silver (#38BDF8) crescents labelled 'Phosphatase' sweep smoothly over the JAKs, receptor tails, and nuclear STAT dimers, peeling off the gold (#FACC15) 'P' tags. The unphosphorylated STATs release from DNA, drift back out of the nucleus into the cytoplasm, and return to the waiting pool.
scenes.narration: Now ask how a healthy signal turns off. Two main brakes do most of that work. First, tyrosine phosphatases strip phosphates from JAKs, receptor tails, and STATs. Once a STAT loses its phosphate in the nucleus, it returns to the cytoplasm, ready for reuse.

scenes.tts: Second, the pathway makes its own brake. Among the genes that Stats switch on are the Socs proteins, suppressors of cytokine signaling. After a delay, Socs proteins dock on the active receptor and Jak. Some block the Jak directly, and several can tag the complex for breakdown.
scenes.caption: Second, the pathway makes its own brake. Among the genes that STATs switch on are the SOCS proteins, suppressors of cytokine signaling. After a delay, SOCS proteins dock on the active receptor and JAK. Some block the JAK directly, and several can tag the complex for breakdown.
scenes.visual: From the violet DNA, violet-plum (#C084FC) shield blocks labelled 'SOCS' emerge after a visible delay (a small clock icon labelled 'Delay'), rise to the membrane, and dock onto the active receptor tail and JAK. One shield covers the JAK's coral kinase lobe (label 'Blocks JAK'); on another complex, small tag beads attach (label 'Tagged for breakdown').
scenes.narration: Second, the pathway makes its own brake. Among the genes that STATs switch on are the SOCS proteins, suppressors of cytokine signaling. After a delay, SOCS proteins dock on the active receptor and JAK. Some block the JAK directly, and several can tag the complex for breakdown.

scenes.tts: A third restraint acts before cytokine even arrives: the pseudokinase lobe on each Jak. In most patients with polycythaemia vera, one amino acid change alters Jak two's pseudokinase. That weakens restraint and helps two Jaks pair. Jak two then fires with little or no erythropoietin, producing too many red cells.
scenes.caption: A third restraint acts before cytokine even arrives: the pseudokinase lobe on each JAK. In most patients with polycythaemia vera, one amino acid change alters JAK2's pseudokinase. That weakens restraint and helps two JAKs pair. JAK2 then fires with little or no erythropoietin, producing too many red cells.
scenes.visual: Remove the amber EPO cytokine from outside the left receptor. Zoom onto the two-lobed JAK2s: show the normal rose (#FB7185) pseudokinase lobe holding the coral kinase off, then flash a small amber highlight dot ('V617F') on the rose lobe. The restraint loosens, the two pseudokinase lobes pull together at their contact face, gold 'P' tags fire across with no EPO outside, and teal STAT pairs stream downward. Label: 'Active without EPO'.
scenes.narration: A third restraint acts before cytokine even arrives: the pseudokinase lobe on each JAK. In most patients with polycythaemia vera, one amino acid change alters JAK2's pseudokinase. That weakens restraint and helps two JAKs pair. JAK2 then fires with little or no erythropoietin, producing too many red cells.

scenes.tts: Missing Jak two silences the erythropoietin receptor; loosening its restraint leaves the kinase stuck on. So receptor tails select specific Jaks and Stats, while brakes restrain signaling. Together, receptor sorting and layered restraint keep a rapid pathway accurate and under control.
scenes.caption: Missing JAK2 silences the erythropoietin receptor; loosening its restraint leaves the kinase stuck on. So receptor tails select specific JAKs and STATs, while brakes restrain signaling. Together, receptor sorting and layered restraint keep a rapid pathway accurate and under control.
scenes.visual: Pull back to a balanced split summary inside the same cell frame: on the left, receptor tails matching specific JAKs and STATs ('Tail sorting'); on the right, pseudokinase restraint, cyan phosphatases, and plum SOCS shields holding the pathway in balance ('Brakes'). Fade cleanly to the end card.
